items.question: The same textual conflict appears once when you merge a branch, but five times when you rebase it onto the same base. Why?
items.answer: A merge performs a single three-way merge, so you resolve the conflict once and record the resolution in one merge commit. A rebase replays each commit onto the new base individually, so every replayed commit that touches the conflicting hunk can raise the same conflict again, and each resolution is baked into that commit's replayed copy (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase). This is why well-scoped commits, or squashing first, reduce rebase pain: fewer replays means fewer chances to resolve the same hunk.
items.trap: The naive answer 'merge and rebase resolve conflicts identically, the history just looks different' fails because the unit of resolution differs: one merge commit resolves the whole conflict once, while a rebase demands a resolution per replayed commit, so identical content can require repeated manual work.

items.question: main has not moved since you created your feature branch. You merge the branch into main and the log shows no merge commit. Why, and what would --no-ff change?
items.answer: When the current branch is an ancestor of the branch being merged, Git fast-forwards: it moves the branch pointer and creates no merge commit, so the feature commits land directly on main's line. `git merge --no-ff` forbids the fast-forward and forces a merge commit even when none is needed, preserving the shape of the feature branch as a visible group with a single revertable merge point (https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Basic-Branching-and-Merging).
items.trap: The naive answer 'merging always creates a merge commit' fails because fast-forward is the default when histories have not diverged; teams that require --no-ff are buying topology and an easy revert point, not correctness.

items.question: During `git rebase main` on your feature branch, a conflicted file offers 'ours' and 'theirs'. Which one is your branch's version?
items.answer: Neither merge intuition applies. The git-rebase documentation is explicit: a rebase replays each commit from the working branch on top of the upstream branch, so when a conflict happens the side reported as 'ours' is the so-far rebased series starting with the base (main), and 'theirs' is the working branch; the sides are swapped relative to a merge (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase). Resolving with `git checkout --ours` during a rebase therefore keeps main's side and discards your own change.
items.trap: The naive answer 'ours is my branch, same as in a merge' fails because rebase replays your commits onto the checked-out base, so the labels invert; resolving with the merge mental model silently deletes your own work while the rebase 'succeeds'.

items.question: When is `git rebase --skip` the right call, and what does it actually do to your work?
items.answer: Skip drops the commit currently being replayed entirely and continues with the next one. It is correct only when that commit's change is already present in the new base, for example when the same patch was applied upstream, so the replay is a guaranteed no-op that conflicts trivially. Before skipping I verify the change really exists upstream, for instance by diffing the commit against the base; otherwise the commit's change is simply gone from the rebased branch (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase).
items.trap: The naive answer 'skip just bypasses the annoying conflict and moves on' fails because skip discards the commit's changes, not just the conflict; if the change was not already upstream, that work vanishes from the branch with no error.

items.question: Trunk-based development integrates into main constantly. How does half-finished work reach main without users seeing it, and what does that demand from the pipeline?
items.answer: Incomplete changes merge behind feature flags or other inert paths: the code deploys continuously, but the behavior stays off or limited to selected contexts until the flag changes. That demands strong automated tests on every integration, flag hygiene (owner, default-safe state, expiration date), and a fast way to turn the flag off. Without that maturity, trunk-based degrades into either a broken main or a pile of permanent flags (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/strategy-cicd-litmus/understanding-cicd.html).
items.trap: The naive answer 'trunk-based means shipping half-finished features to users' fails because the decoupling is deliberate: code integration is continuous, behavior exposure is controlled by flags, and the pipeline has to guarantee both.

items.question: A team wants release control, so it keeps one long-lived branch per environment (dev, staging, main) and cherry-picks fixes between them. What problems does that create?
items.answer: Cherry-picking copies a change as a new commit identity, so the same logical fix exists several times and the branches drift apart; later merges re-encounter those changes as conflicts or duplicates. Release gating has moved from the deployment system (pipelines, promotions, approvals) into branch topology, which is harder to audit and slower to roll back. The guidance is to keep one main source of truth and put release control in the delivery pipeline rather than in branch proliferation (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/choosing-git-branch-approach/choosing-git-branch-approach.html).
items.trap: The naive answer 'more branches give more control over releases' fails because branches are a code-integration tool, not a deployment gate; duplicating commits across environment branches creates drift and merge pain that the pipeline was supposed to prevent.

items.question: A pipeline deploys every green build of main automatically to staging, but production requires a human approval. Is that continuous deployment?
items.answer: No, it is continuous delivery: every build is automated and production-ready, but promotion to production keeps an explicit approval gate. Continuous deployment removes that gate so a green build reaches production with no human decision. The distinguishing factor is the approval, not the amount of automation (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/strategy-cicd-litmus/understanding-cicd.html).
items.trap: The naive answer 'if deploys are automated, it is continuous deployment' fails because both models automate deployment; what separates them is whether the last step into production still requires a human approval.

items.question: Why do mature pipelines build one artifact and promote it through environments instead of rebuilding per environment, and what breaks if you rebuild?
items.answer: The artifact that passed the tests must be the artifact that ships. A rebuild is not guaranteed to be identical: dependency resolution can drift when versions are not pinned, build metadata differs, and the fresh build can even fail or pick up changed source. Rebuilding per environment means the bits verified in staging are not provably the bits running in production, which destroys the audit chain from test to release (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/strategy-cicd-litmus/understanding-cicd.html).
items.trap: The naive answer 'rebuilding is safer because each environment gets fresh bits' fails because freshness is exactly the risk: the guarantee you want is that tested bits and shipped bits are the same bits.

items.question: In a multi-stage build, do the earlier stages' layers end up in the final image, and what exactly does `COPY --from=build` transfer?
items.answer: No. Each FROM starts an independent stage and only the last stage becomes the image; earlier stages exist only while building. `COPY --from=build` copies files out of that stage's filesystem into the final stage as an ordinary new layer; it does not import or reference the build stage's layers (https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/).
items.trap: The naive answer 'multi-stage squashes everything into one image, so build tools must be cleaned up manually' fails because the isolation is structural: the final image never contains the earlier stages' layers, which is precisely why multi-stage shrinks images and attack surface without cleanup scripts.

items.question: Why does the reviewed Dockerfile copy package*.json and run npm ci before copying the source, and what happens to build time if you copy everything first?
items.answer: Docker caches layers in order and invalidates everything from the first instruction whose inputs changed. With the manifests copied first, the npm ci layer is reused as long as the package files do not change, so a source-only edit skips dependency installation entirely. If `COPY . .` comes first, every source edit also invalidates the install layer and npm ci reruns on each build (https://docs.docker.com/build/concepts/dockerfile/).
items.trap: The naive answer 'instruction order is a style preference' fails because order is the caching contract: any change placed before the install step re-runs it, turning a seconds-long rebuild into a minutes-long one.

items.question: A job uses `${{ secrets.PROD_KEY }}`, but PROD_KEY is stored in the protected production environment and the job does not declare that environment. What does the job get?
items.answer: The secret is simply not available: environment secrets are exposed only to jobs that reference the environment and pass its protection rules, such as required reviewers and branch restrictions (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/deployment-environments). There is no parse-time error and no automatic fallback; the value is not injected, so the failure surfaces later, typically as an authentication error against the deploy target. Declaring `environment: production` on the job is what brings both the gate and the secret into scope.
items.trap: The naive answer 'secrets are workflow-global so it just works' fails because scoping is the point of environments: without the reference, neither the approval gate nor the secret applies, and the resulting failure looks like a broken deploy rather than a missing environment.

items.question: A debug step printed a secret into a job log and GitHub redacted it. Is the leak contained?
items.answer: No. GitHub automatically redacts secret values printed to workflow logs, but the documentation is clear that because a value can be transformed in multiple ways, for example substrings or encodings, the redaction is not guaranteed (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/secrets). Anyone with access to the log may also hold surrounding context. The correct response is to remove the logging step, treat the secret as exposed, and rotate it.
items.trap: The naive answer 'GitHub masked it, so nothing escaped' fails because redaction is a display convenience, not containment; transformed fragments of the value can appear unmasked, so the safe assumption is that it leaked and must be rotated.

items.question: With a private bucket and Origin Access Control, what happens when a user requests the object's s3.amazonaws.com URL directly, bypassing CloudFront?
items.answer: S3 returns Access Denied. The bucket policy grants s3:GetObject only to the cloudfront.amazonaws.com service principal, with an AWS:SourceArn condition pinning the grant to that specific distribution, so every other principal, including an anonymous browser request to the S3 endpoint, is refused (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html). That is the design goal: the bucket is unreadable except through the distribution, so TLS, caching, and edge-level restrictions cannot be bypassed.
items.trap: The naive answer 'OAC makes the objects public so both URLs work' fails because OAC exists for the opposite reason: it lets the distribution read a private bucket, keeping every non-CloudFront path denied.

items.question: Your build hashes asset filenames, but index.html keeps the same key on every deploy. What should the pipeline invalidate, and what is the cost of invalidating /* each time?
items.answer: Hashed assets are immutable: a new build produces new keys and the old keys can stay cached. Only the HTML entry point, and anything else stored under a stable key, needs invalidation, so the pipeline should invalidate that path or give it a short TTL or a versioned key. Invalidating /* works but flushes every object at every edge location, which is slower, consumes invalidation capacity, and throws away warm cache for content that did not change (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html).
items.trap: The naive answer 'always invalidate everything to be safe' fails because it trades away CloudFront's core benefit: it evicts unchanged, still-valid objects at every edge location, slowing the deploy and consuming invalidation capacity for no correctness gain.

items.question: You added a method in the API Gateway console, but the stage URL still behaves like the old API. Why?
items.answer: A stage points at a deployment, which is a snapshot of the API at the moment it was deployed. Console edits change the API's definition but do not touch the stage until you create a new deployment to it. The same applies to infrastructure-as-code changes: the tool updates the API definition, and the stage only moves when a deployment is created or updated (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-apigateway-tutorial.html).
items.trap: The naive answer 'API Gateway changes go live immediately' fails because the stage is a frozen snapshot; without an explicit redeploy, the stage keeps serving the previous version of the API no matter what the console shows.

items.question: A caller gets a 403 on an IAM-authorized method. Which of the two permission paths do you investigate first?
items.answer: The two paths fail differently. With IAM authorization, the caller's identity needs execute-api:Invoke on the API's execution ARN, and an explicit deny anywhere wins; a failure on this path is the 403. Separately, API Gateway needs permission to invoke the Lambda integration, granted through the function's resource policy or an appropriate service role; a failure on that path typically surfaces as a server error from the integration, not as the caller's 403. Separating the paths avoids the classic wrong fix of granting the caller lambda:InvokeFunction (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/permissions.html).
items.trap: The naive answer 'grant the caller lambda:InvokeFunction' fails because it confuses the principals: the caller invokes the API (execute-api:Invoke), while API Gateway, not the caller, is the principal that invokes Lambda.

items.question: A role's trust policy names your CI system as a trusted principal. Does that trust policy define what the pipeline can do in your account?
items.answer: No. The trust policy answers only who may assume the role; what the assumed role may do is defined by its permission policies. The pipeline's effective power is the combination: it must be allowed to assume the role, and then everything it does is capped by the role's permissions. Reviewing only one of the two documents always gives a false picture of access (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/security-iam.html).
items.trap: The naive answer 'the permissions live in the trust policy' fails because trust and permission are separate documents answering separate questions; a role can trust everyone and allow nothing, or trust one principal and allow everything.

items.question: You tightened a deployment role and the next deploy failed at runtime, even though the change plan reviewed cleanly. Why does static review of the policy JSON miss this, and what catches it?
items.answer: IAM evaluates each request when it happens. A policy that omits an action only fails when a code path actually makes that call, and nothing in the JSON reveals which calls the deploy will make. What catches it is exercising the real flows: running the deployment in a lower environment, reading the deny from the error output or logs, and iterating until observed access matches the policy. That is why least privilege is an operating process of review and removal, not a one-time JSON exercise (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/security-iam.html).
items.trap: The naive answer 'I read the policy and it looks right' fails because permissions are proven at request time; an action that is needed but missing is invisible until the exact code path runs, so only exercised flows and logs reveal the gap.

items.question: `terraform apply` fails halfway through creating resources. What does the infrastructure look like now, and what does Terraform do about it?
items.answer: Terraform does not roll back. The resources created before the failure exist and are recorded in state, which is written incrementally as the apply progresses, so the partial state is accurate. The correct response is to read the error, fix the cause, and apply again: the next plan sees the partially created set and proposes only the remaining changes. Assuming apply is transactional is the dangerous mistake, because it leads to orphaned, billed resources that nobody cleans up (https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/state).
items.trap: The naive answer 'Terraform is transactional, so a failed apply leaves everything as it was' fails because applies are incremental: half-created infrastructure is real and recorded in state, and pretending otherwise orphans resources.

items.question: CI generated and reviewed tfplan on the pull request. Another change merged to main before the apply job ran `terraform apply tfplan`. What gets applied?
items.answer: The saved plan is what gets applied: applying a plan file executes the changes captured when the plan was generated, not a fresh plan of the current configuration (https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/apply). That is the mechanism that makes the reviewed change the applied change, and it is also the trap: if the configuration moved on, the applied plan no longer matches the repository, and the next run will show a diff. This is why the core workflow tells teams to review the final concrete plan after merge, since merge order and recent changes can alter it (https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/intro/core-workflow). Robust pipelines generate the plan from the exact commit being promoted, or re-plan after merge and review that final plan.
items.trap: The naive answer 'apply always uses the latest configuration' fails because a plan file argument pins the apply to the saved plan; review parity and staleness risk are the same mechanism, so the plan must come from the commit you actually ship.

items.question: A flag has been fully on for three months. What does it cost to leave it on, and what does removing it actually involve?
items.answer: Leaving it on accrues flag debt: every flag adds a runtime decision path, extra test combinations, and a configuration dependency that can fail independently of the code. Removing a temporary flag is a code change: delete the dead path and the flag wiring, adjust the tests, and ship it, which itself needs review, deployment, and a rollback plan. That is why every temporary flag should be created with an owner and an expiration date, so cleanup is scheduled work instead of archaeology (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/strategy-cicd-litmus/understanding-cicd.html).
items.trap: The naive answer 'a flag that is on is free, it is just an if statement' fails because the cost is the permanent second code path, the larger test matrix, and the added runtime dependency; removal is a real deployment with its own risk, which is exactly why flags need expiration dates.

items.question: The flag evaluation service is unavailable at request time and the flag's configured default is off. What should the application do?
items.answer: Fail safe to the default: serve the known-good path with the flag off, degrade gracefully, and surface the evaluation failure in metrics instead of failing the request. This is why the default state must be chosen for safety rather than novelty: the default is what runs during outages, bad configurations, and first deployments. Failing open, meaning treating the outage as 'on', couples your release exposure to the flag service's uptime (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/strategy-cicd-litmus/understanding-cicd.html).
items.trap: The naive answer 'fail open so users still get the new experience' fails because it turns the flag service into a runtime dependency of your release exposure: when it breaks, every flag silently ships.

items.question: Blue/green promises rollback by switching traffic back to blue. When is that promise false?
items.answer: The traffic switch is only a rollback if blue is still intact and both versions are compatible at the data layer. If green ran a backward-incompatible schema migration or wrote records blue cannot read, routing traffic back does not undo the data: blue now fails on the same records. This is why the choice hinges on state and schema compatibility, and why green must be verified with real traffic shapes before the switch, with a tested way to return traffic to the known-good version (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/deployment-type-bluegreen.html).
items.trap: The naive answer 'blue/green means rollback is always instant' fails because only the traffic switch is instant; data written by green is not undone by routing, and an incompatible schema change can break blue itself.

items.question: A canary at 10% ran for 10 minutes with no alarms, so it was promoted to full traffic. On a low-traffic service, why might that prove nothing?
items.answer: Alarms need enough requests to be statistically meaningful. Ten percent of a low-traffic service for ten minutes can be a handful of requests, far below any error-rate threshold, so a badly broken build can pass a 'clean' canary. The canary percentage and bake time must be chosen against real traffic volume and monitoring quality, and a canary only measures what is actually instrumented; on low traffic you need longer bake times or synthetic traffic before shifting (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/deployment-configurations.html).
items.trap: The naive answer 'no alarms during the canary window means safe' fails because absence of alarms can mean absence of data: with too few requests, thresholds never trigger, and the promotion proceeds on a sample that could not detect the failure.

mcqs.question: You are on main and run `git merge feature`. main has not moved since feature branched off it. What does Git do by default?
options: It creates a merge commit so the feature branch topology is preserved in the history
It fast-forwards: main simply moves to feature's tip and no merge commit is created
It rebases feature's commits onto main and then advances main
It reports that everything is already up to date and leaves main unchanged
mcqs.explanation: When the current branch is an ancestor of the branch being merged, Git just moves the pointer (a fast-forward) and creates no merge commit; `git merge --no-ff` exists precisely to force a merge commit in this situation (https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Basic-Branching-and-Merging). The strongest distractor is the merge-commit one: many candidates believe merging always produces a merge commit, but that only happens when the two histories have actually diverged. 'Already up to date' confuses this with the case where the branch being merged has nothing new, and the rebase option confuses merging with rebasing.

mcqs.question: You run `git rebase main` while on your feature branch and a conflict stops the rebase. In this conflict, which side is 'ours'?
options: main: rebase replays your commits on top of the new base, so the base is 'ours' and your replayed commits are 'theirs'
your feature branch: 'ours' always means the branch you had checked out when you started
origin/main, because a rebase always contacts the remote first
whichever side Git resolved automatically in the previous replayed commit
mcqs.explanation: The git-rebase documentation states it directly: a rebase replays each commit from the working branch on top of the upstream branch, so when a conflict happens the side reported as 'ours' is the so-far rebased series starting with upstream and 'theirs' is the working branch; the sides are swapped relative to a merge (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase). The strongest distractor is the feature-branch one: carrying the merge mental model into a rebase makes people resolve every conflict to the wrong side and silently discard their own changes. The remote option is wrong because rebase works on local refs, and the previous-commit option describes no real mechanism.

mcqs.question: A pipeline automatically deploys every green build of main to staging, but a human approval is required before production. What is this pipeline?
options: Continuous deployment, because every successful build is deployed automatically
Continuous integration, because the pipeline builds and tests every commit
Continuous delivery: builds reach a production-ready state automatically, but promotion to production keeps an explicit approval gate
Neither, because real CD pipelines must use canary or blue/green releases
mcqs.explanation: The dividing line is the production gate: continuous delivery keeps production promotion approvable, while continuous deployment removes that explicit approval so every green build goes live (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/strategy-cicd-litmus/understanding-cicd.html). The strongest distractor is continuous deployment: candidates equate 'automated deploys' with it, but the human approval before production is exactly the gate that continuous deployment eliminates. Continuous integration names the build-and-test feedback loop all these models share, and the canary option confuses deployment strategies with the delivery/deployment distinction.

mcqs.question: In a multi-stage Docker build, which statement about the final image is true?
options: It contains only the final stage's layers; earlier stages exist during the build, and COPY --from copies files out of them into the final stage
It contains every stage's layers, which is why you must manually uninstall build tools in the last stage
It contains only the files copied with COPY --from, without any base image of its own
It contains the build stage plus a small diff layer that references the build stage at runtime
mcqs.explanation: Each FROM starts an independent stage and only the last stage becomes the image; COPY --from pulls files out of an earlier stage's filesystem into the final one as an ordinary layer, and the earlier stages are then discarded (https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/). The strongest distractor is the every-stage-layers one: it applies the single-stage mental model, where manual cleanup would indeed be needed; multi-stage exists precisely so build tools never reach the final image. The diff-layer option invents a runtime link between stages that does not exist, and the no-base-image option forgets the final stage's own FROM.

mcqs.question: Why does a well-ordered Dockerfile copy package*.json and run the dependency install before copying the application source?
options: Because npm ci refuses to run when application source files are already present in the layer
Layer caching: Docker reuses cached layers up to the first instruction whose inputs changed, so source-only edits skip the expensive install step
Because it keeps the application source out of the build stage entirely
Because multi-stage builds require the dependency step to be the first RUN instruction
mcqs.explanation: Docker builds layers in order and invalidates the cache from the first changed instruction onward; if the manifests are copied and installed first, a source edit only invalidates from COPY . . onward and the install layer is replayed from cache (https://docs.docker.com/build/concepts/dockerfile/). The strongest distractor is 'it keeps the source out of the build stage': the source is copied on the very next line, so nothing is excluded; the ordering is about cache invalidation, not image content. The npm ci refusal is false (it only needs the manifests), and the multi-stage syntax requirement is invented.

mcqs.question: In GitHub Actions, the secret PROD_DEPLOY_KEY is stored in the protected production environment, which requires two reviewers. A job uses ${{ secrets.PROD_DEPLOY_KEY }} but never declares `environment: production`. What happens?
options: The workflow fails to parse, with an unknown-secret validation error before any job starts
The job pauses and asks the two reviewers for approval, then receives the secret
The secret is not available to the job: environment secrets are exposed only to jobs that reference the environment and pass its protection rules
The job fails immediately at runtime with a 'secret not found' error
mcqs.explanation: Environment secrets are scoped to jobs that declare the environment; a workflow job cannot access environment secrets until the environment's required approvers have approved, and a job that never references the environment gets neither the gate nor the secret (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/deployment-environments, https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/secrets). The strongest distractor is the approval one: the protection rules protect the environment, they do not reach out to unrelated jobs. There is no parse-time validation of secret names, and an unavailable secret is simply not injected, so the failure surfaces later, typically as an authentication error, not as an immediate 'secret not found'.

mcqs.question: A static site is served by a CloudFront distribution whose origin is a private S3 bucket using Origin Access Control. A user opens the bucket's s3.amazonaws.com object URL directly in a browser. What does S3 return?
options: Access Denied: the bucket policy allows only the CloudFront service principal, and only for that specific distribution
A redirect to the equivalent CloudFront URL
The object, because OAC makes bucket content readable through any AWS endpoint
Access Denied, but only until CloudFront has cached the object at the nearest edge location
mcqs.explanation: With OAC the bucket stays private: the bucket policy grants s3:GetObject to the cloudfront.amazonaws.com service principal with an AWS:SourceArn condition pinning it to that distribution, so any other request, including a direct browser hit on the S3 endpoint, is denied (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html). The strongest distractor is 'the object, because OAC makes content readable': OAC exists for the opposite purpose, letting the distribution read a private bucket so viewers cannot bypass CloudFront. The cache-dependent option invents an authorization model that does not exist; authorization is evaluated on every request.

mcqs.question: You add a new resource and method to a REST API in the API Gateway console, but requests to the stage URL still behave like the old API. The Lambda function is unchanged. What is the most likely cause?
options: API Gateway's response cache is serving stale responses for the new method
The API has not been deployed to the stage: a stage serves a snapshot, and console edits take effect only after a new deployment
The Lambda execution role needs to be recreated after API changes
IAM policy propagation delay; the change appears after a few minutes
mcqs.explanation: A stage points at a deployment, which is a snapshot of the API at deploy time; editing resources or methods changes the API definition but does not update the stage until you deploy to it again (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-apigateway-tutorial.html). The strongest distractor is the response cache: API Gateway does have an optional response cache, but it is disabled by default and caches responses, not the API's routing structure, so a brand-new method missing at the stage is a snapshot problem. The execution-role and propagation options describe unrelated mechanisms that would not make a new method invisible.

mcqs.question: An IAM role's trust policy lists a principal in another AWS account. What does that trust policy alone let the other account do?
options: Perform any action the role's permission policies allow, without assuming the role
Read all resources in the account that owns the role
Nothing, until action-level Allow statements are also added to the trust policy
Assume the role; once assumed, they can do only what the role's permission policies allow
mcqs.explanation: The two documents answer different questions: the trust policy answers who may assume the role, and the permission policies answer what the assumed role may do (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/security-iam.html). The strongest distractor is 'perform any action without assuming the role': trust is not permission; the external principal must actually assume the role, and even then its effective power is capped by the role's permissions. The action-level-Allows option misreads the trust policy; the action it authorizes is sts:AssumeRole itself. The read-all-resources option invents implicit access that no policy granted.

mcqs.question: In CI you run `terraform plan -out=tfplan` and a reviewer approves the output. Another change is merged to main before the apply job runs `terraform apply tfplan`. What is applied?
options: The changes captured in tfplan: applying a plan file executes the saved plan, not a fresh plan of the current configuration
A fresh plan of the merged configuration, because apply always re-plans by default
An error: Terraform refuses to apply a plan generated from an older commit
Both changes: Terraform merges the saved plan with the new configuration
mcqs.explanation: Applying a saved plan file executes exactly the changes captured when the plan was generated; that is what makes the reviewed change and the applied change correspond (https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/apply), and it is why the core workflow warns that a plan reviewed on a pull request can differ from the final plan after merge (https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/intro/core-workflow). The strongest distractor is the fresh-plan one: apply without an argument does plan-then-apply in one step, but with a plan file argument there is no re-planning, which is both the review-parity feature and the staleness risk. The error and merge options describe behavior that does not exist.

mcqs.question: A feature flag is in a 50% progressive rollout. The same end user reloads the page twice. What determines whether they see the same variation both times?
options: Random assignment per request, so about half of all reloads flip the experience
Server-side session affinity, which the flag service maintains for you
Context bucketing: the flag service sorts contexts into consistent groups based on a chosen randomization unit such as user or device, so the same context keeps getting the same variation
The rollout percentage applies only to first-time users; everyone else keeps whatever they saw first
mcqs.explanation: Progressive rollouts use randomized traffic allocation and context bucketing: contexts are sorted into consistent groups based on a randomization unit like user, device, or account, and within a rollout a customer's variation changes only once, in one direction (https://launchdarkly.com/docs/home/releases/progressive-rollouts.mdx). The strongest distractor is the per-request randomness one: that is exactly the failure mode bucketing exists to prevent, because flipping users between code paths mid-session breaks experience consistency and pollutes measurements. The session-affinity and first-time-user options attribute state-keeping to mechanisms the flag service does not provide for percentage rollouts.

scenarios.prompt: A teammate ran this sequence and now claims the rebase 'ate their feature'. Diagnose what actually happened to their changes and how to recover the pre-rebase state.

code.code:
git checkout feature/payment-flow
git rebase main
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/checkout.ts
git checkout --ours -- src/checkout.ts   # "keep my version"
git add src/checkout.ts
git rebase --continue
# ...the same pattern for three more conflicts...
git rebase --continue
git log --oneline -5
# 4 commits replayed, but src/checkout.ts now matches main

scenarios.modelAnswer:
What actually happened: during `git rebase main`, Git checks out main as the new base and replays the feature commits on top, so in every conflict 'ours' is main's side and 'theirs' is the teammate's own commit; the git-rebase documentation states the sides are swapped relative to a merge (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase). By resolving every conflict with `git checkout --ours`, they kept main's version and discarded their own changes in each conflicted file, while the replayed commits still carry their original messages. The rebase 'succeeded': the history looks right and the content is wrong, which is the worst combination because nothing fails loudly.

Recovery: the pre-rebase commits still exist. Rebase creates new commits and leaves the old ones reachable from the reflog, and ORIG_HEAD points at the pre-rebase tip (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-reflog):

  git reflog                     # find the entry before 'rebase (start)'
  git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD     # or: git reset --hard HEAD@{n}

Then redo the rebase resolving conflicts properly: inspect each conflicted file, edit it to the intended combined result, `git add` the file, and `git rebase --continue`. At any point, `git rebase --abort` returns the branch to its untouched pre-rebase state. Because the branch was rewritten, coordinate before force-pushing if others had already pulled it.
rubric: Correctly identifies that during a rebase 'ours' is the new base (main) and 'theirs' are the replayed feature commits, the inverse of a merge.
Explains the silent consequence: the replayed commits keep their messages but the conflicted files now carry main's content.
Recovers via the reflog or ORIG_HEAD and a hard reset, rather than hand-reconstructing the damaged history.
Re-runs the rebase with the inspect, edit, add, continue sequence, and knows that abort restores the pre-rebase state.
Mentions coordinating before force-pushing a rewritten branch that others may have based work on.

scenarios.prompt: This workflow is meant to promote the tested build to production behind an approval. The secret PROD_DEPLOY_KEY is stored in the protected production environment, which requires two reviewers. Find every defect in the deploy job and refactor it.

code.code:
name: release
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: web-dist
          path: dist

  deploy-production:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci && npm run build
      - name: Debug deploy config
        run: echo "Deploying with key prefix ${PROD_DEPLOY_KEY:0:8}"
        env:
          PROD_DEPLOY_KEY: ${{ secrets.PROD_DEPLOY_KEY }}
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh production
        env:
          PROD_DEPLOY_KEY: ${{ secrets.PROD_DEPLOY_KEY }}

scenarios.modelAnswer:
Defect 1: the deploy job never declares `environment: production`. Two consequences: the environment's protection rules (required reviewers, branch restrictions) never apply, so nothing actually gates production; and the environment secret is not exposed to this job at all, because environment secrets are available only to jobs that reference the environment and pass its rules (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/deployment-environments). The deploy runs with no credential, and the common 'fix' of copying the secret to repo level would permanently remove the gate.

Defect 2: the deploy job rebuilds from source (`npm ci && npm run build`) instead of consuming the artifact the build job produced and tested. What ships is a new build, not the tested bits: dependency resolution can drift and the tested artifact and the deployed artifact are no longer provably the same. Promote the artifact instead.

Defect 3: the debug step prints a prefix of the secret. GitHub automatically redacts secret values printed to logs, but the redaction is not guaranteed for transformed values such as substrings (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/secrets). Treat the token as leaked: delete the step and rotate the key.

Refactored deploy job:

```yaml
  deploy-production:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production   # brings the approval gate and the secret into scope
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: web-dist
          path: dist
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh production
        env:
          PROD_DEPLOY_KEY: ${{ secrets.PROD_DEPLOY_KEY }}
```

The approval stays as an explicit production gate (continuous delivery), the exact tested artifact is what ships, and the secret is scoped to the one job that needs it.
rubric: Adds environment: production and explains that protection rules and environment secrets apply only to jobs that reference the environment.
Replaces the rebuild with an artifact download so the tested artifact is the one promoted (build once, promote the same bits).
Removes the debug echo and treats the printed token as leaked, noting that automatic redaction is not guaranteed for transformed values like substrings, so the key must be rotated.
Keeps production promotion as an explicit approval gate instead of removing it.
Mentions least privilege for the deploy credential: scoped to the deploy, rotatable, and auditable.

scenarios.prompt: Security review flagged this image: it runs as root, an npm token shows up in the image build metadata, the image ships with devDependencies and source code inside, and every source-only change reinstalls dependencies. Refactor the Dockerfile and explain each fix.

code.code:
FROM node:22
WORKDIR /app

ARG NPM_TOKEN
COPY . .
RUN echo "//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=${NPM_TOKEN}" > .npmrc \
  && npm install \
  && rm .npmrc

RUN npm run build
ENV NODE_ENV=production
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

scenarios.modelAnswer:
Problem 1, single stage: devDependencies, build tooling, and the whole source tree ship in the production image. Split into a build stage and a runtime stage; only the final stage's layers end up in the image, and COPY --from carries just the build output (https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/).

Problem 2, cache order: `COPY . .` precedes the install, so any source edit invalidates the install layer. Copy package*.json first, install, then copy the source (https://docs.docker.com/build/concepts/dockerfile/).

Problem 3, the token: build arguments and environment variables are inappropriate for secrets because they persist in the final image, and deleting .npmrc in the same RUN does not scrub the ARG value from the build history. Use a BuildKit secret mount, which exposes the secret only for the duration of that RUN (https://docs.docker.com/build/building/secrets/). The exposed token must be rotated.

Problem 4, root and base image: run as the non-root `node` user and use a minimal base such as node:22-alpine.

Problem 5, reproducibility: `npm install` resolves versions ad hoc; use `npm ci` with the committed lockfile.

Refactored:

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token \
  npm config set //registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken "$(cat /run/secrets/npm_token)" \
  && npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

The token now exists only inside the build stage's single RUN, never in a layer of the final image, and the runtime stage carries only production dependencies plus the built output.
rubric: Separates build and runtime stages and explains that only the final stage's layers ship, dropping devDependencies, source, and build tooling.
Reorders the COPY instructions so manifests and install come before the source, restoring layer caching for source-only changes.
Eliminates the ARG token and explains why deleting the file in a later step does not scrub it; uses a BuildKit secret mount and rotates the exposed token.
Runs the runtime as a non-root user on a minimal base image.
Switches to lockfile-driven npm ci for reproducible installs.

scenarios.prompt: State lives in a remote backend that supports locking. This single job is supposed to guarantee that only reviewed Terraform changes reach production. Predict what actually happens when two pull requests merge an hour apart, then fix the pipeline so the applied change is the reviewed one.

code.code:
jobs:
  terraform:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: terraform init
      - name: Show the plan for reviewers
        run: terraform plan -out=tfplan
      - name: Apply after merge
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        run: terraform apply

scenarios.modelAnswer:
What actually happens:

1. `terraform apply` runs with no plan file, so it re-plans from the current configuration and state and applies that. The tfplan generated for reviewers is never consumed: it is not persisted anywhere and apply ignores it anyway. What gets applied is whatever the configuration looks like at apply time, which can differ from what was reviewed, because merge order and recent infrastructure changes can alter the final plan (https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/intro/core-workflow).

2. With two merges an hour apart, each push to main triggers this job. The backend lock serializes concurrent state writes, so overlapping runs do not corrupt state, but locking does nothing for review parity: the second run's plan includes the first run's changes plus its own, and nobody reviewed that combination.

3. A failed apply is left half-done: Terraform does not roll back partial changes, state records what was actually created, and the team must fix the cause and re-apply deliberately.

Fix:

```yaml
jobs:
  plan:
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: terraform init
      - run: terraform plan -out=tfplan
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: tfplan
          path: tfplan

  apply:
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: terraform init
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: tfplan
          path: tfplan
      - run: terraform apply tfplan
```

Applying the saved plan file executes exactly the reviewed change (https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/apply). Two details matter: the plan must be generated from the exact commit being promoted (the pull request's merge commit), otherwise the saved plan is stale relative to main; and if the team prefers to absorb late merges, the alternative is to re-plan after merge and review that final plan before applying, which is what the core workflow recommends. The production environment gate keeps the apply behind an approval.
rubric: Identifies that terraform apply without a plan file re-plans, so the applied changes can differ from what reviewers saw.
Persists the plan artifact and applies that exact file, generated from the commit being promoted.
Explains what state locking does and does not prevent: concurrent state writes are serialized, but review parity is not protected.
Knows that a failed apply leaves partial changes with no automatic rollback, and defines the response (fix and re-apply; state records the partial set).
Recognizes the staleness tradeoff of saved plans and gates the apply behind an environment approval.
